title: Schatten and Frobenius norms
subtitle: G2 lecture 057000 · expanded companion
adaptation: Standalone slide treatment of the spoken lecture and display-only mathematical appendix; authored derivations, worked calculations and local SVG diagrams.

slides.title: One operator, several notions of size
slides.lead: Schatten norms turn the singular-value list of a map into familiar ℓₚ measurements.
body: For a finite-dimensional map A:E→F, choose its nonnegative singular values. The Schatten p norm aggregates their pth powers, while the endpoint p=∞ keeps only the largest one.

The key examples are the nuclear norm at p=1, the Hilbert–Schmidt or Frobenius norm at p=2, and the operator norm at p=∞. They have different interpretations but depend on the same invariant singular-value data.
slides.takeaway: Schatten norms are ℓₚ norms of singular values.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 057000 · One operator, several notions of size

slides.title: A rectangular worked example
slides.lead: Take A from ℝ² to ℝ³ with columns (3,0,0) and (0,4,0).
body: The source Gram matrix is diag(9,16), so the singular values are four and three. Consequently the nuclear norm is seven, the Frobenius norm is five, and the operator norm is four.
For p=4 the norm is the fourth root of 4⁴+3⁴=337. There is no requirement that A be square: its stretching is still completely described by those two values.
slides.takeaway: One rectangular matrix produces several consistent but different size measurements.

slides.title: Frobenius norm is the total column energy
slides.lead: Choose any orthonormal basis (eᵢ) of the source space.
body: Adding ||Aeᵢ||² over the basis gives the trace of the source Gram operator A* A. The trace also equals the sum of the eigenvalues of A* A, which are the squared singular values.
This proves the Frobenius formula without assuming that the basis consists of singular vectors and explains why the result is coordinate invariant.
slides.takeaway: The Frobenius norm aggregates squared output lengths over any orthonormal input basis.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 057000 · Frobenius norm is the total column energy

slides.title: The trace-norm identity
slides.lead: The modulus |A| is the positive square root of A* A.
body: Its eigenvalues are the singular values, so its trace is their sum. This gives the nuclear norm ||A||S₁=tr|A| even for a rectangular A, because |A| acts on the source space.
This identity must not be confused with tr(A* A), which is instead the square of the Frobenius norm. The two traces carry different powers of the singular values.
slides.takeaway: Trace of the modulus and trace of the Gram operator encode different norms.

slides.title: Why these measurements satisfy norm axioms
slides.lead: Nonnegativity, scalar homogeneity, and definiteness come directly from the singular-value formula.
body: The triangle inequality requires more structure: singular values of A+B are weakly majorized by the componentwise sum of singular-value lists, and ℓₚ is a symmetric gauge for p≥1.
The weak-majorization comparison and ordinary ℓₚ triangle inequality together yield the Schatten triangle inequality. This also explains why p below one does not give a norm.
slides.takeaway: Triangle inequalities come from weak majorization and convex ℓₚ gauges.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 057000 · Why these measurements satisfy norm axioms

slides.title: Compare the three endpoints
slides.lead: For a nonnegative singular-value list, the maximum is no larger than the ℓ₂ norm, which is no larger than the ℓ₁ sum.
body: These are elementary list inequalities transferred to matrix norms. When the rank is r, Cauchy–Schwarz also gives an upper bound for ℓ₁ by √r times ℓ₂.
Keeping the dependence on rank visible prevents a dimension-free claim when the singular-value list grows.
slides.takeaway: Rank controls how far aggregate norms can exceed the largest singular value.

slides.title: Why unitary coordinates do not matter
slides.lead: A unitary change of input or output coordinates leaves all singular values unchanged.
body: If A is replaced by UAV*, the source Gram operator becomes V A* A V*, a unitary conjugate of the original Gram matrix. It therefore has the same eigenvalues.
Every Schatten p norm stays unchanged under these transformations. This is why the formulas are intrinsic measurements of a linear map, not of one matrix presentation.
slides.takeaway: Unitary invariance is a consequence of Gram-eigenvalue invariance.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 057000 · Why unitary coordinates do not matter

slides.title: What each norm reveals geometrically
slides.lead: The operator norm, Frobenius norm, and nuclear norm ask different questions of the same map.
body: The operator norm records the worst single stretch. The Frobenius norm records the root of total squared stretch energy. The nuclear norm sums all stretches and is sensitive to how many directions participate.

For perturbations of spectral subspaces, the operator norm measures a maximal angle while the Frobenius norm can aggregate many orthogonal rotations. We choose a norm to match the quantity we want to control.
slides.takeaway: A norm selection expresses which geometry the bound is intended to measure.
slides.eyebrow: G2 · 057000 · What each norm reveals geometrically

slides.title: A second rectangular check
slides.lead: A single nonzero singular value gives equality of all three endpoint measurements.
body: For a rank-one matrix with singular values (5,0,0), nuclear, Frobenius, and operator norms are all five. In contrast, the map with singular values (4,3) has measurements 7,5,4.
This contrast shows that the spread between norm values is controlled by the number and distribution of nonzero singular directions.
slides.takeaway: Rank-one maps eliminate the difference between these three measures.

slides.title: Reconstruct the formulas
slides.lead: Start from a rectangular SVD and the positive Gram operator.
body: Derive the squared Frobenius formula by summing ||Aeᵢ||² across an orthonormal input basis, then identify tr|A| as the nuclear norm. Evaluate both formulas for the map with singular values four and three.
Finally, prove the endpoint comparisons using ordinary ℓ₁, ℓ₂, and ℓ∞ inequalities. The same proof works in any pair of finite-dimensional inner-product spaces.
slides.takeaway: The Gram operator, trace, and singular values give three views of the same data.
